en: The Sūtra on the Fundamental Causes of Conditions Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Craving is deep and profound; though its outward manifestation has not yet arisen, it remains bound and submerged within. It also has a root and a basis; it does not come about without a cause."

Craving involves indulgence and excess; its root lies in being fully developed. To undergo the state of madness and intoxication, lacking clear contemplative understanding, is called the root of delusion (*moha*).
That which arises conditioned by delusion is likewise the root of existence (*bhava*).
"What is the root? The dazzling of forms and sounds, and the wandering delusions of the five hindrances—these are the roots of ignorance.
The obscuration and darkness of the five hindrances lead to shadows and lingering hesitation; these, too, have a root."
What constitutes the root?
The牵引 (qian-yin, drawing forth) of the three evil seeds is what is called the root.
"The cultivation of the three evil sprouts also has a root."
What constitutes the root?
Not restraining the faculties and consciousnesses is also a root.
"Not restraining the faculties and consciousnesses" serves as the basis for the conditions that lead to existence.
What constitutes the root?
It refers to that which is not worthy of mindfulness, yet one waits for it incessantly; this is called the root.
"That which is not worthy of mindfulness also arises from its own causal conditions; it is not without a root."
What constitutes the root?
Not following right faith and being deluded as to one's direction—this is called the root.
"Lacking faith and following error also has causes that lead to it; it is not without a root."
What constitutes the root?
Being led astray by an evil teacher and listening to and receiving what is not the Dharma—this is called the root.
Even when there is no formal loss of hearing, there is likewise a causal root.
What constitutes the root?
To oppose and turn away from the assembly of sages and eminent heroes—this is called the root.
That such discord with the sages and eminent heroes leads to this opposition also has its root.
What is the root? To lose the quality of reverent upholding, the emptying of the mind, and the gathering of joy—this is called the root.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

Now, when one loses the company of the wise—a gathering of the pure and lofty—their conduct of body, speech, and mind becomes clouded by delusions of sight and hearing, and their inner heart is stifled and blocked.
Through such unrighteous views, their faith and inclination are destroyed.

When one turns one’s back on the Right Path, false views increase; when false views increase, internal restraint is lost; when internal restraint is lost, the three evils arise unchecked; when the three evils arise unchecked, the five hindrances fill one up; when the five hindrances fill one up, the root of delusion becomes complete; when the root of delusion is complete, craving and grasping flourish. Through this process, the seeds of rebirth are sown, attachment to existence increases, and defilements become boundless.
"The transcendent, clear wisdom that ascends to the essential point of liberation also has its foundation.
What is meant by the foundation for the liberation of transcendent wisdom?
It is the excellence of the seven factors of enlightenment; these are said to be the means of reaching that foundation."
“The mirror of the seven factors of enlightenment also has its basis.
What is this basis? It is the four foundations of mindfulness; these are the basis of enlightenment.”
"The four bases of mental power (ṛddhipāda) arise from having a foundation; they do not exist without a foundation.
Wherein lies their meaning?
It is said that they are pure, clean, and sublime, and their practice resides in three things."
"The three types of pure conduct also have a basis; they do not lack a basis.
What is the meaning of this 'basis'?
It refers to guarding and restraining the sense faculties—this is the basis."
"Guarding and restraining the sense faculties also has a foundation; it is not without a foundation.
What is the meaning of this 'foundation'?
It refers to the mirror-like reflection and profound illumination—this is the foundational mindfulness."
"When fundamental mindfulness illuminates the past, it likewise has a basis, which leads through conditions to entry into the correct [path].
What is this basis? Fundamental mindfulness creates excellence; this is called 'planting faith.'"
"Faith also has a basis; it is not without a basis.
What is the basis of faith?
It is the extensive learning of the sūtras, the sequence of the Path, and the essential principles of the scriptures—this is called the basis."
"Hearing the teachings of the sutras also has its foundation; it is not without foundation.
What is meant by hearing the Dharma?
It refers to those who practice the conduct of the worthy, whose actions are pure, and whose deeds are true."
"The purity of the wise also has its root. What is its root?
It is said to be the accumulation of sublime conduct that is pure and immaculate."

"Thus it is, bhikṣus! The noble one assembles excellence by relying upon wisdom; he serves those who are learned and establishes the foundation of faith. Once the foundation of faith is established, he attains right mindfulness. When right mindfulness is cultivated, he guards and restrains his sense faculties. Once the sense faculties are guarded, he ascends to the purity of the three types of conduct. Having attained these three purities, he practices the four foundations of mindfulness. Once the four foundations of mindfulness are established, the seven factors of enlightenment arise.
When the seven factors of enlightenment are fully realized, this is unconditioned liberation and transcendence from the world."

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the disciples received and practiced it. This concludes the *Pratītyasamutpāda-hṛdaya-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Essence of Dependent Origination) as taught by the Buddha.
